content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a Unet structure for fourier neural operators (FNOs). FNOs are quite widely used, albeit quite often mostly as a convenient baseline, as they turn out not to work overly well in many settings. Along the lines of classic Unets, this paper proposes to improve this by including skip connections alongside different levels of upsampling to preserve information from the inputs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
As a main strength of this paper I think that - as far as I can tell - FNOs with Unet skip connections haven't been used. As such, it is interesting to see how well they fare. The evaluation is also nicely presented, and includes a good variety of existing Unet architectures and alternatives. 

In terms of weaknesses, the extension of FNOs with skip connections is very straight forward. As such, the level of technical complexity of the contributions is not very high, and there are no additions on the theoretical side (which would be fine, of course, if the former is given). Also the two test cases that are used are relatively simplistic (one is presented with 2 variations, which however yield an identical ordering of the different methods).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
While there are significant differences in terms of the performance of the different methods that were evaluated, the regular FNOs don't fare too well. And while it's great that the authors honestly present the performance of the FNO-Unets, they don't seem to consistently outperform the regular Unets.

In terms of presentation, I would also recommend to include qualitative side-by-side comparisons for the different methods. The MSE values can hide a lot of missing structures. (E.g., evaluating the different methods in terms of spectral content could also be interesting.)
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is a nice read, and trying skip connections in FNOs is definitely not a bad idea. However, given their negligible improvements over regular Unets, and the limited scope of the submission, I'm hesitant to recommend it for publication at ICLR. In its current form it seems more suitable for a smaller conference or workshop. From an ICLR paper, I would expect either more substantial technical and/or theoretical contributions that yield more significant improvements.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides an extensive study of Fourier and U-Net based architectures for modelling temporal PDEs. It considers existing UNet based architectures inspired from computer vision for multi-scale spatiotemporal modelling and extends them by integrating FNO layers in early blocks to perform frequency filtering before downsampling. These architectural changes are compared to representative Fourier based neural PDE surrogates (FNO and UNO) on two different settings: (i) fixed and (ii) varying PDE parameters and time scales for which it shows strong performance of UNets over FNO. The code will be open-sourced and can be used to further investigate and compare neural PDE surrogates.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

* This paper provides an extensive and thorough experimental comparison of UNet and FNO-based methods on challenging PDE datasets with varying parameter and time-scales. The open-source code will likely have practical use by allowing comparison with strong UNet baselines for PDE modelling. 
* It presents interesting observations for UNet and FNO models based on these experiments: improved UNets outperform FNO, adding FNO blocks to UNet architectures seems overall beneficial, UNet-conditioned architectures work better across parameters and timescales than FNO-based counterparts. 

**Weaknesses and questions**

* *Novelty*: Overall, this paper lacks a general strong message: it appears like a comparison between existing methods on new experimental settings / PDE datasets. The novelties in terms of model are limited: architecture changes for UNets inspired from computer vision were introduced in Ma et al. (2021) and Chen & Thuerey (2021) (cf references p5) which were reimplemented and the existing UNO model is only slightly modified using these strong backbones (Fourier blocks only on some blocks in U-FNet and not all).
* *U-FNet vs UNO*: Filtering before downsampling is an interesting idea, especially with motivation from signal processing. Yet, why is it useful to only replace the early UNet blocks by FNO layers and not all as in UNO (especially as U-F2Net > U-F1Net on Shallow water)? Experimentally, adding the results of either a UNO with a $\text{UNet}_{\text{mode}}$ backbone or a U-F1Net/U-F2Net with the UNet backbone in UNO would be more convincing to show the difference between the U-FNet and UNO models independently of the considered UNet backbone.
* *Lack of interpretation and explanation of results*: *1) U-FNet results*: why are there improvements on Shallow-water but degradations on Navier-Stokes velocity? *2) “Connecting Fourier transform and convolution”*: it would be good to better explain Figure 3: why is the number of modes different in each block? Also how come the pattern is similar across UNet blocks? I would assume the different blocks to process the input differently thus to have different patterns.
* *Conditioning on time-scale*: why is it necessary to encode timescale into the architectures given that p6 “inputs to the neural PDE surrogates were respective fields at previous t timesteps”? Neural Operators defined over a spatial and temporal domain are resolution invariant in both time and space c.f. FNO paper. Which FNO model is considered: FNO-3D or the auto-regressive formulation in FNO-2D?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**
Overall the paper is clear yet it lacks interpretation of experimental results and explanations for some choices (listed above in **Weaknesses and questions**).

**Quality and reproducibility**
The quality of the experimental evaluation is strong and is the main strength of this paper. Reproducibility is encouraged with the appendix and the code provided in the supplemental materials. 

**Novelty**
See bullet point *Novelty* above (**Weaknesses and questions**)
content.summary_of_the_review:
The empirical results of this paper are interesting. The open-source code can have some practical use for comparing neural PDE surrogates: it reimplements strong UNet architectures for PDE modelling and considers challenging PDE datasets with varying parameters and timescales. Yet, the novelties of this paper are limited: the UNet architectures used in this paper already exist (or with minor change of the number of down / upsampling layers); moreover, the proposed U-FNet model has minor practical difference with UNO and the advantages of adding only some Fourier Layers instead of all to a given UNet backbone is not demonstrated. This is why I recommend borderline reject.

====Post rebuttal====

I thank the authors for their response and for clarifying my questions. I agree with the authors that the proposed UNet variations could help benchmarking current PDE surrogate models by serving as strong baselines (validated by a thorough and convincing experimental evaluation) for the proposed datasets / tasks (or possibly other ones). Yet I feel that the novelty issues outweigh the empirical evidence; combining UNet architectures and Fourier layers already exists in UNO (though with an older UNet architecture); authors provided some evidence that adding only some layers can be enough, yet, this feels like a minor technical contribution. I thus maintain my initial score.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a comparison between several existing different PDE solving methods using neural networks on specific fluid dynamics problems, where physical effects occurring on different time and spatial scales can have a dramatic effect on the solutions, making generalization between scales an important requirement. The authors also combine elements of these existing methods to produce marginally better performing architectures. Finally, the authors promise a useful code database for comparing PDE solvers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1) The paper is clearly written, and seems to be well aware of its context within existing literature.
2) The experimental setups seem sound and the results correspond to phenomenological considerations used to build the architectures described.

Weaknesses:
1) It is unclear to me whether an empirical review of this kind (comparing two types of network for very specific PDEs) is sufficiently interesting for the audience of ICLR.
2) While the authors present a rational (global and local information regarding the solutions) for combining FNO layers into U-Nets, this rational is not further explored, i.e. providing some measure to understand what local/global information is being utilized by these layers, even empirically.
3) The performance improvement stemming from the only novel construction is marginal in some cases, and is non-existent in others, making the paper more of a review on some test cases rather than a conceptual novelty.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear and well written, though I fail to see the true novelty in it, aside from an empirical one.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is clear and well written, though I am unsure of the novelty and relevance of this paper's contribution, as it focuses only a specific subclass test case of PDEs (albeit very important one) where scale generalization is important, as well as mostly demonstrating results for existing networks. There is only a slight modification to these constructions which does not dramatically improve performance, nor proving or empirically exploring why it is expected to do so.

content.title: General response
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for the constructive feedback. We are glad that reviewers found the paper well-written, and the experimental comparisons extensive. However, in this general response, we want to address the main criticism regarding the lack of novelty. 

Neural PDE modeling is a relatively young field, and as such currently very much suffers from non-consistent or even non-existing baselines. The baselines in literature are not very clear and given the success of U-Net like approaches in image modeling tasks, the "demonstrated" under-performance on PDE surrogate modeling is somewhat surprising. 

Comparisons of popular FNO based PDE surrogates and modern U-Nets are missing in the literature, or are done only for weak version of the U-Net, e.g. a 2015  U-Net with `tanh` activations is used in the recently released PDEbench paper (while using `gelu` for FNO) [1], 2015 U-Nets with unclear details are used by Stachenfeld et al in "Learned Coarse Models for Efficient Turbulence Simulation” [2], by Dang et al in "TNT: Vision Transformers for Turbulence Simulations" [3], and by Li et al in "Fourier Neural Operators" [4]. 

In this paper, we don't just aim for presenting yet another neural PDE surrogate architecture. We rather ablate a huge variant of possibilities which arise when looking at ResNet, Dilated ResNet, Fourier and U-Net architectures. Towards this end, our presented architectural combinations are thought to close the search space, yielding an overall better understanding. Making sure our baselines are strong, allowed us to make meaningful progress towards better PDE surrogate models in the form of U-F[*]Nets bringing the signal-processing perspective on how Fourier layers could play a role. 

Taking parameter counts, memory efficiency, training and forward time, as well as performance on various datasets into account, U-(F)Net based architectures seem to be the architectures to favor which is not that surprising when looking at computer vision results. 

The second point we are trying to make is that neural PDE surrogates should be tested against their capabilities to generalize over equations and equation parameters. This complements PDE modeling schemes such as e.g. Deep O-Net by Lu et al which aim to generalize for continues output grids. These generalizations can take advantage of sophisticated text conditioning approaches as done for image/video generation. Towards this end, it is very interesting to see how different architectures react to conditioning experiments. 

To complete our case studies, we have added many different experiments: 

1. We have included more FNO baseline runs, to allow for even more comprehensive comparisons. 
2. We included a second training objective, namely the normalized L2 loss as used by Li et al to train Fourier Neural Operators. 
3. We have included Dilated ResNet models, introduced by Stachenfeld et al which also provide a possibility for incorporating global information. 
4. We have included the U-Net model as in the PDEbench paper. 
5. We have included alternative parameter conditioning models (Spatial-Spectral) to make conditioning in FNO blocks more competitive. 
6. We have included peak GPU memory usage estimates. 
7. We have updated and modified all tables and respective plots. 
8. We have included U-F3Net runs with specs to make the distinction to UNO architectures clearer. 

 

We will opensource a properly documented data generation, datasets, training procedures, as well as all our approximately 20 different model implementations, such that people can start using competitive models as baselines for future PDE surrogates. 

Finally, we understand that novelty of architectures themselves can be seen as limited. However, good science and future progress in the field is contingent on having good baselines. Moreover, given the popularity of U-Net architectures especially for modern diffusion models, they would likely see increased attention on improving their performance both from software and hardware perspective. We find that the same U-Nets (and some minor modified versions) perform consistently well for very different PDEs, especially as we focus on _generalization_. Similarly treating time as conditioning variable gives an alternative route to learning longer horizon predictions compared to expensive and unstable auto-regressive training popular in current PDE surrogate modeling literature. Future PDE surrogate models would do well to consider these trade-offs and make proper comparisons.

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.15275 

 

[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04616 

 

[4] https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.08895
